passages.happening:
“Therefore let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in God, instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment” (verses 1-2).

“And this we will do, if God permits” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The writer has just said his readers are still on milk. Now, instead of waiting for them to catch up, he says: let us go on.

‘Leave’ does not mean throw away. A builder does not tear up the foundation. He leaves it in place and builds on it. The writer names six foundation stones in three pairs: repentance and faith; washings and the laying on of hands; the resurrection of the dead and God's final judgment.

Every one of these had roots in the Jewish faith the readers knew. Jews practised ritual washings and laid hands on people for blessing and on sacrifices, and many believed in the resurrection and the judgment. The word ‘baptisms’ is plural, and it is not the usual word for Christian baptism. So it may mean teaching about the difference between Christian baptism and other washings. For readers tempted to fall back, these shared foundations felt safe. The writer wants them to build higher.

‘Repentance from dead works’ means turning away from deeds that lead to death, or from deeds done without life in them.

‘Let us go on’ is, in Greek, ‘let us be carried on’. It suggests being carried by God's power, not only straining by our own effort. And so he adds, ‘if God permits’. Growth is God's gift.
passages.ot:
The six foundations are rooted in Israel's Scriptures. Repentance is the call of all the prophets: “Repent and turn from all your transgressions” (Ezekiel 18:30). Faith in God goes back to Abraham, of whom it is written, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).

The law of Moses had many washings for cleansing (Leviticus 15 and 16). The laying on of hands was used when a sacrifice was offered (Leviticus 1:4), and when Moses commissioned Joshua (Numbers 27:23).

And the hope of resurrection and judgment is spoken in Daniel: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.asks: A foundation is for building on. Ask whether you are still laying the same foundation again and again, or whether you are building. Ask what ‘maturity’ would look like for you this year. And ask God for it, since growth comes ‘if God permits’.

passages.happening:
Now comes the most frightening warning in the letter.

“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age— and then have fallen away—to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame” (verses 4-6).

Then a picture from farming. “For land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended receives the blessing of God. But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. In the end it will be burned” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
In Greek, verses 4 to 6 are one long sentence. It describes one group of people from five sides. They were ‘enlightened’, the word Hebrews uses later for the readers' own coming to faith (10:32). They ‘tasted the heavenly gift’. They ‘shared in the Holy Spirit’. They ‘tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age’, the miracles and gifts that came with the gospel (2:4). Then comes the turn: ‘and then have fallen away’. The word means to fall aside, to defect. It appears only here in the New Testament.

‘Crucifying the Son of God all over again’ means treating Jesus as if he deserved the cross, siding with those who put him to death. ‘Subjecting Him to open shame’ means holding him up to public scorn. This is not a person who sins and is sorry. It is a person who has turned against Christ himself.

Then the picture. Two fields get the same rain. One grows a good crop. The other grows only thorns and thistles. In the ancient world a farmer would burn off a worthless field. The point is fruit: what grows after God has poured out his gifts.

This passage has had a troubled history. In the early church some used it to argue that serious sins committed after baptism could never be forgiven by the church. And many tender-hearted people since have read it and been terrified that it was about them.
passages.ot:
The picture of the two fields comes from the Bible's first pages. After Adam's sin, God said, “cursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17), and “Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you” (Genesis 3:18).

The prophets used the same kind of picture for God's people. Isaiah sang of God's vineyard: “He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour!” (Isaiah 5:2). In its own setting it is God's lament over Israel and Judah, spoken by a prophet to his own people, calling them back.

And ‘tasted the goodness of the word of God’ echoes a psalm: “Taste and see that the LORD is good” (Psalm 34:8).

The wilderness generation of chapters 3 and 4 stands behind this passage too. They had seen God's wonders and eaten his bread, and still they turned back.
passages.hard:
‘It is impossible ... to be restored to repentance.’ Does this mean a true Christian can fall away and never come back?

Few passages have been read in so many ways. Here are the main readings, each as its holders would put it. These notes do not choose.

Much of the Reformed and Baptist world reads it in one of a few ways. Many hold that the people described had real experiences of the gospel among believers, light, gifts, the Spirit's work around them, but were never truly born again; like the field of verses 7 and 8, they received much and bore no real fruit. Others hold that the warning is spoken to true believers and describes a real outcome, and that God uses such warnings to keep his people, so that those who hear them hold on. Some read it as a case put forward to show that falling away could never be undone, without saying that it ever happens.

Much of the Wesleyan and Arminian world reads the words as describing real believers, who can fall away by settled unbelief and be lost. Many of them read the ‘impossible’ as applying to a deliberate and final turning away from Christ, not to every believer who slides back. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that grace can be lost through grave sin and restored through repentance, and reads the verse as a warning about the hardened state of those who reject Christ.

One detail helps many readers. ‘They themselves are crucifying the Son of God’ can also be read ‘while they are crucifying’ him: repentance is impossible for as long as a person goes on rejecting Christ.

Whatever view one holds, two things are plain. The warning is about turning against Christ himself, not about everyday failure or honest struggle. And the writer's goal is to keep his readers from it; in the next breath he says, ‘we are convinced of better things in your case’ (verse 9). The note on Romans 8:31-39 and the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’, set out the main views more fully.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: This warning is meant to be heard, not explained away. Ask whether there is any part of you turning against Christ, not merely failing him. Ask what is growing in the field of your life after so much rain. And if this passage frightens you, ask whether the very fact that you care is a sign of the tenderness toward God that it says is gone in those it describes.

passages.t: ‘We are convinced of better things in your case’
passages.happening:
At once the tone changes.

“Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case—things that accompany salvation. For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints and continue to do so” (verses 9-10).

“We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure. Then you will not be sluggish, but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
‘Beloved’ is the only time the writer calls them that in the whole letter. He has just said something terrible, and now he wants them to hear his heart. The warning is real, but it is not his verdict on them.

Why is he so sure? Because he has seen their love. They had served ‘the saints’, their fellow believers, and they were still doing it. God, he says, ‘is not unjust’: he will not forget. The writer is not saying they earned salvation by serving. He is saying their love is a sign of God's work in them, the ‘things that accompany salvation’.

Readers in different traditions hear verse 9 in different ways. Reformed readers often see it marking the readers off from the fruitless field of verse 8: their lives show the signs of salvation. Arminian readers often hear it as the writer's confidence that the readers have not fallen away and need not. Either way, it is a word of hope.

Then he urges them on. ‘This same diligence to the very end.’ ‘Sluggish’ is the same word as ‘dull’ in 5:11. They have not become sluggish in love; he does not want them to become sluggish in hope. And he points them to models: those who ‘through faith and patience’ inherit the promises. Abraham comes next, and chapter 11 is full of them.
passages.ot:
‘God is not unjust’ is the faith of the Old Testament: “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just” (Deuteronomy 32:4). God sees and remembers kindness: “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (Proverbs 19:17).

The call to patient hope runs all through the psalms: “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” (Psalm 27:14).
passages.asks: After the warning comes the word ‘beloved’. Ask whether you hear both. Ask where your love for other believers has shown itself, and whether it has grown cold. And ask whose faith and patience you could learn from, someone who has waited a long time and kept trusting.

passages.t: God's oath: an anchor for the soul
passages.happening:
The writer now gives the firmest ground for hope he can find: God's own promise, backed by an oath.

“When God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself, saying, ‘I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants.’ And so Abraham, after waiting patiently, obtained the promise” (verses 13-15).

“Men swear by someone greater than themselves, and their oath serves as a confirmation to end all argument. So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath. Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged” (verses 16-18).

“We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world an oath settled an argument. A person swore by a god or by something greater than himself, calling down judgment if he lied. God has no one greater to swear by, so he swore by himself.

The ‘two unchangeable things’ are God's promise and God's oath. God's word alone would have been enough. But, out of kindness, God added an oath, so that his people could be completely sure. The word ‘impossible’ comes back here: it is ‘impossible for God to lie’. The same word that warned in verse 4 now comforts.

‘We who have fled to take hold of the hope’ pictures someone running to a place of refuge.

Then the anchor. Hope holds the soul steady, like an anchor holds a ship in a storm. But this anchor is not dropped into the sea. It is fixed in heaven, ‘behind the curtain’, in the inner room where God is. The anchor became an early Christian sign, scratched on walls in Rome.

And Jesus is there as ‘forerunner’, a word for a scout who runs ahead so that others can follow. Israel's high priest went behind the curtain alone, once a year, and came out again. Jesus went in ‘on our behalf’, and others will follow him in. The chapter ends with Psalm 110:4 again, ready for chapter 7.
passages.ot:
The promise comes from Genesis 22, after Abraham was willing to offer Isaac: “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son, I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore” (Genesis 22:16-17). Abraham waited many years for the son God had promised, and he saw the promise begin to be kept.

The Law speaks of places of refuge where a person could flee for safety; Israel was told to “designate cities to serve as your cities of refuge” (Numbers 35:11).

‘Behind the curtain’ is the language of the Day of Atonement, when the high priest went “inside the veil” into the Most Holy Place (Leviticus 16:12).

And the chapter ends where chapter 5 did, with the psalm: “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).
passages.hard:
Jesus told his followers not to swear oaths at all (Matthew 5:34). Why does God swear one here?

Jesus was warning against the habit of using oaths to make some promises seem more binding than others, as if ordinary words could be bent. His point was that his followers should be people whose plain ‘yes’ means yes. God's oath is the opposite of that habit. God's word was already completely true. He added an oath not because his promise needed it, but because his people did. He was stooping to their weakness, speaking in the way people understood, so that they would be ‘strongly encouraged’.

Christians differ on whether Jesus' words forbid all oaths, such as an oath in court. The Anabaptists of the 1500s refused all oaths, and some Christians still do. Most churches have held that Jesus forbids careless and dishonest swearing, not a solemn oath when the law asks for one, and they point to this very verse. The note on Matthew 5:33-37 sets out both. These notes do not choose. The point here is God's kindness: he makes his promises as sure as they can possibly be.
passages.asks: Your hope is anchored where Jesus has gone. Ask what storms are pulling at you now, and what you have been anchoring your hope to. Ask what it would mean to trust a God who swore by himself for your sake. And ask whether you have ‘fled to take hold’ of that hope, or are still standing outside the refuge.
